- Mammogram (diagnostic if there are symptoms) if the last one was more than 12 months ago.
- Cervical screening if not up to date.
- Spirometry with post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC to confirm the COPD diagnosis, and an alpha-1 antitrypsin level and phenotype (guidelines recommend testing all patients with COPD, and her low pack-year history makes it more relevant).

**3. Targeted imaging and endoscopy**
- Colonoscopy within 4 weeks if she has never had one or is not up to date. At age 57 she should already have been screened. If FIT is positive, she has iron-deficiency anemia, or she has GI symptoms, escalate to within 2 weeks.
- Upper endoscopy if there is iron-deficiency anemia, dyspepsia, dysphagia, early satiety, weight loss or epigastric symptoms. Do it urgently (within 2 weeks).
- CT chest/abdomen/pelvis with contrast if any of the following is present: red-flag symptoms, abnormal labs (anemia, raised LDH, abnormal LFTs or calcium), a node or mass on exam, an abnormal chest x-ray, acanthosis nigricans or tripe palms, or rapid progression of the skin lesions. Do not order it routinely if everything is negative, but keep a low threshold. She does not meet USPSTF low-dose CT screening criteria (20 pack-years), so use diagnostic imaging only when indicated.

**4. Dermatology referral (urgent, within 2 weeks)**
- Ask for dermoscopy of the lesions and biopsy of any atypical, pigmented or changing lesion, since melanoma can hide among SKs. Ask them to confirm the diagnosis and look for acanthosis nigricans, tripe palms or other paraneoplastic signs.
- Do not treat the lesions as a cosmetic problem until the work-up is done.

**5. Contingencies with thresholds**
- Any abnormal test, mass or suspicious finding: refer urgently to the relevant specialty (GI, breast surgery, pulmonology or oncology, as appropriate), seen within 2 weeks, and arrange tissue diagnosis.
- Anemia (Hb <12 g/dL) or low ferritin: urgent GI evaluation with both upper and lower endoscopy.
- Weight loss of 5% or more over 6 months, or new GI or respiratory symptoms: go straight to CT chest/abdomen/pelvis and endoscopy without waiting for the 3-month visit.
- All initial work-up negative: do not discharge. Re-examine at 3 and 6 months, then every 6 months for 2 years (the sign can precede the cancer by months to years), and repeat targeted evaluation if SKs keep increasing or new symptoms appear.
- If a malignancy is found: SKs often regress with treatment, and reappearance may suggest recurrence. Document this in the chart.
- Biopsy shows melanoma or another skin cancer: same-week dermatology-oncology or surgical referral.

**6. Follow-up schedule**
- 1-2 weeks: results review and exam findings (me).
- 4-6 weeks: confirm that colonoscopy, mammogram, dermatology and any other studies have been completed and the reports received.
- 3 months: repeat history, exam, weight, skin photographs and CBC/CMP (me).
- 6 months, then every 6 months for 2 years: repeat as above. Ask dermatology for review at 6 months.
- Track every referral until the result is in the chart.

**7. Counseling**
- Explain that SKs are benign, but a sudden crop can rarely signal an internal problem, so you are checking for it, and that most people with eruptive SKs turn out not to have cancer.
- Advise her not to pick, scratch or shave off lesions. Itchy lesions can be treated with emollients, and a lesion that is symptomatic or irritated can be treated by cryotherapy or curettage by dermatology after the work-up. Cosmetic removal is not covered by insurance and not urgent.
- Advise sun protection (broad-spectrum SPF 30+, protective clothing).
- Tell her to report any lesion that bleeds, darkens, grows quickly, looks asymmetric or has multiple colors.

**8. Return precautions**
- Come in within a few days for: unintentional weight loss, persistent abdominal pain, change in bowel habits, rectal bleeding or black stools, difficulty swallowing, persistent cough or change in cough, a breast lump, night sweats, swollen glands, new dark velvety skin patches or thickened palms, a rapid increase in lesions, or severe itching.
- Go to the ED for: coughing up significant blood, vomiting blood, heavy black or bloody stools, severe abdominal pain, or severe breathlessness not relieved by her inhaler.

**9. COPD care (concurrent)**
- Confirm spirometry and stage with GOLD classification. Use a short-acting bronchodilator as needed, and escalate to a LAMA or LAMA/LABA if she has persistent symptoms (mMRC ≥2 or CAT ≥10) or exacerbations.
- Review inhaler technique.
- If she is still smoking, advise cessation firmly and offer pharmacotherapy (varenicline, or nicotine replacement) plus counseling. If she has quit, reinforce this.
- Vaccines: annual influenza, current COVID-19, pneumococcal conjugate (PCV20 or PCV21), RSV (single dose, indicated at ages 50-59 with chronic lung disease), and Tdap if not up to date.
- Offer pulmonary rehabilitation if she is symptomatic.
- Refer to pulmonology if spirometry is inconsistent with her smoking history, AAT is low, or the chest imaging is abnormal.

**10. Knee osteoarthritis**
- Start with exercise (strengthening, low-impact aerobic activity), weight management if applicable, and physical therapy if needed.
- Topical diclofenac 1% gel, 4 g per knee up to four times daily, is first line. Use acetaminophen up to 3 g/day as needed.
- Avoid routine oral NSAIDs for now. If one becomes necessary, use the lowest dose for the shortest time and check renal function and GI risk, noting that GI bleeding would confound the cancer work-up.
- Reassess at each visit. Refer to orthopedics only if pain becomes refractory or function declines. This is not urgent.

**11. Documentation and communication**
- Tell the patient who is responsible for each pending result and how you will contact her.
- Make sure she has my clinic's contact number for any new symptoms between visits.

## Recommendation set 2

This is not an emergency, but an abrupt eruption of numerous seborrheic keratoses over months is not something to dismiss as routine aging. It may be benign (“pseudo–Leser-Trélat”), but the pattern can rarely be associated with an occult malignancy, particularly gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma or hematologic malignancy, and warrants prompt confirmation and targeted evaluation.

1. **Arrange dermatology assessment promptly—ideally within 2–4 weeks.**  
   - Request a **full-body skin examination** to confirm that the lesions are truly seborrheic keratoses and to look for atypical lesions, melanoma, acanthosis nigricans, or other paraneoplastic skin findings.  
   - Dermatology should perform **dermoscopy and shave/punch biopsy of any lesion that is atypical** (asymmetric, irregularly pigmented, ulcerated, bleeding, rapidly enlarging, painful, or diagnostically uncertain). Typical seborrheic keratoses do not require biopsy or removal.

2. **Perform a focused review for cancer-related symptoms and a complete physical examination at the next primary-care visit, preferably within 1–2 weeks.**  
   Specifically ask about unintentional weight loss, anorexia/early satiety, dysphagia, persistent reflux, abdominal pain, change in bowel habits, rectal bleeding/melena, iron-deficiency symptoms, lymph node enlargement, fevers/night sweats, new cough, hemoptysis, breast symptoms, or postmenopausal bleeding. Examine lymph nodes, abdomen, breasts as appropriate, and assess for hepatosplenomegaly.

3. **Ensure that routine evidence-based cancer screening is current; do not order broad “tumor-marker” panels or whole-body imaging solely because of seborrheic keratoses.**  
   - **Colorectal cancer:** If she is not up to date, arrange **screening colonoscopy now** (preferred if never screened or if there are gastrointestinal symptoms), or annual **fecal immunochemical test (FIT)** if colonoscopy is declined/unsuitable. A positive FIT requires diagnostic colonoscopy.  
   - **Breast cancer:** Obtain a **screening mammogram now if none within the prior 2 years**, or follow local screening intervals.  
   - **Cervical cancer:** Confirm adequate screening through age 65: primary high-risk HPV testing every 5 years, HPV/Pap cotesting every 5 years, or cytology every 3 years, depending on prior results and local practice.  
   - **Lung cancer:** She does **not** meet usual annual low-dose CT screening criteria on the stated 10-pack-year exposure; annual screening LDCT is generally reserved for adults aged 50–80 with at least a 20-pack-year history who currently smoke or quit within 15 years. Obtain chest imaging only if symptoms or examination findings warrant diagnostic evaluation.

4. **Escalate diagnostic evaluation if concerning symptoms, examination findings, abnormal screening tests, or abnormal biopsy results emerge.**  
   - Obtain **CBC with differential and comprehensive metabolic panel** if there are constitutional symptoms, bleeding symptoms, adenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or other clinical concern.  
   - Refer to **gastroenterology urgently** for dysphagia, GI bleeding, iron-deficiency anemia, persistent vomiting, early satiety, unexplained weight loss, or abnormal colorectal screening; endoscopy and/or colonoscopy should then be directed by symptoms.  
   - Refer to **hematology/oncology urgently** for unexplained lymphadenopathy, cytopenias, persistent night sweats/fevers, hepatosplenomegaly, or suspicious pathology.  
   - Consider diagnostic CT imaging only when supported by symptoms, abnormal examination, labs, or specialist assessment—not as indiscriminate screening.

5. **Review medications and timing of the eruption.**  
   Document all prescription, over-the-counter, supplement, and recently started medications. Some medications and inflammatory skin conditions can produce eruptive or “pseudo–Leser-Trélat” patterns; the temporal relationship may help dermatology determine whether medication withdrawal or substitution is appropriate. Do not stop essential medication without the prescriber’s guidance.

6. **Treat the seborrheic keratoses only if symptomatic or cosmetically bothersome.**  
   - Typical lesions are benign and need no medical therapy.  
   - Dermatology can offer cryotherapy, curettage/electrodessication, or shave removal for irritated lesions; counsel that these procedures can cause pigment change, blistering, scarring, and recurrence/new lesions elsewhere.  
   - Avoid over-the-counter “mole removers,” acids, or home freezing kits on uncertain lesions.

7. **Optimize COPD care, particularly smoking cessation.**  
   - Confirm current smoking status and offer cessation treatment if she still smokes. A reasonable first-line option, if no contraindication and after shared decision-making, is **varenicline 0.5 mg orally once daily for days 1–3, then 0.5 mg twice daily for days 4–7, then 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks**, with a quit date during the first 1–2 weeks. Behavioral counseling should accompany medication.  
   - Confirm diagnosis/severity with **spirometry with bronchodilator testing** if not previously documented, review inhaler technique, exacerbation history, oxygen saturation, and current maintenance therapy.  
   - Ensure she has an appropriate rescue inhaler if needed; for example, **albuterol HFA 90 mcg, 1–2 puffs every 4–6 hours as needed** for wheeze or dyspnea, if not already prescribed and if clinically appropriate.  
   - Update COPD-relevant immunizations: annual influenza vaccine, current COVID vaccine, pneumococcal vaccination per local schedule (often PCV20 alone or PCV15 followed by PPSV23), recombinant zoster vaccine, Tdap every 10 years, and RSV vaccination is appropriate to discuss because chronic lung disease increases risk.

8. **Manage mild bilateral knee osteoarthritis conservatively.**  
   - Encourage low-impact strengthening/aerobic exercise, quadriceps strengthening, weight management if applicable, supportive footwear, and consideration of physical therapy.  
   - For pain, if no NSAID contraindication, use **diclofenac 1% topical gel: apply 4 g to each painful knee up to four times daily as needed** (maximum total topical diclofenac 32 g/day). Use the lowest effective dose and avoid applying to broken skin.  
   - Knee radiographs are not needed unless there is trauma, major effusion, locking, instability, marked deformity, or a change in the typical pain pattern.

9. **Give clear return precautions.**  
   Seek prompt review for ongoing rapid appearance of lesions, lesions that bleed, ulcerate, become painful, or change pigment/shape; unexplained weight loss; persistent fatigue; black or bloody stools; new abdominal symptoms; dysphagia; breast lump; postmenopausal bleeding; enlarged lymph nodes; persistent cough; or hemoptysis. Seek urgent care for severe shortness of breath not relieved by rescue inhaler, chest pain, cyanosis, confusion, or rapidly worsening respiratory symptoms.

## Recommendation set 3

Seborrheic keratoses are common, benign growths at this age, but **many new lesions appearing over a few months should not simply be dismissed as normal aging**. This pattern raises the possibility of the **sign of Leser–Trélat**, a rare and imperfectly established association with internal malignancy; it warrants evaluation, but does **not** establish that she has cancer.

1. **Diagnosis and its severity**
   - Working diagnosis: **eruptive seborrheic keratoses**, pending examination to confirm that the lesions are truly seborrheic keratoses.
   - Ordinary seborrheic keratoses are harmless and do not require treatment. Rapid proliferation can occur without cancer, but a convincing eruption—especially with marked itching, weight loss, or gastrointestinal symptoms—deserves assessment for an underlying condition.
   - Neither mild knee osteoarthritis nor COPD explains this eruption based on the information supplied. The presentation alone is not an emergency.

2. **Tests to confirm, exclude dangerous alternatives, and establish treatment baselines**
   - **Arrange an in-person primary care assessment within 1–2 weeks.** Establish the onset, approximate number of new lesions, progression, itching, bleeding, and any recent medication changes; compare with prior photographs if available.
   - Perform a full skin examination, including assessment for atypical pigmented lesions, lymphadenopathy, and new extensive acanthosis nigricans. Review for unintentional weight loss, appetite loss, early satiety, dysphagia, abdominal pain, gastrointestinal bleeding, altered bowel habits, persistent cough changes, hemoptysis, and postmenopausal bleeding.
   - **Dermoscopy** is appropriate to confirm typical lesions. **Biopsy any diagnostically uncertain, irregularly pigmented, ulcerated, persistently bleeding, or otherwise atypical lesion** to exclude melanoma or another skin cancer. Typical lesions do not all need biopsy.
   - There is **no blood test that confirms Leser–Trélat**. If examination supports a genuinely abrupt, extensive eruption, a **CBC with differential and comprehensive metabolic panel** are reasonable initial tests for anemia or other abnormalities that would guide further evaluation; normal results do not exclude malignancy.
   - Verify and complete overdue, age-appropriate screening:
     - **Colorectal cancer:** at age 57, screen if not current; options include annual FIT or colonoscopy every 10 years for an average-risk patient. A positive FIT requires colonoscopy. Symptoms or iron-deficiency anemia require diagnostic evaluation rather than screening FIT.
     - **Breast cancer:** screening mammography if not current, generally every 2 years at her age.
     - **Cervical cancer:** if she has a cervix and is not current, use an appropriate local screening pathway, such as primary high-risk HPV testing every 5 years.
     - **Lung cancer:** the reported **10-pack-year history does not meet standard US eligibility for screening low-dose CT**, even with COPD. Respiratory red flags would instead warrant diagnostic assessment.
   - **Do not routinely order tumor markers, PET scans, whole-body CT, or upper endoscopy solely because of these lesions.** Further testing should follow symptoms, examination, laboratory abnormalities, and dermatology assessment. No medication-specific baseline testing is needed unless treatment is subsequently chosen.

3. **Medications to start, stop, hold, or adjust**
   - **None indicated for the eruption before diagnosis.** No medicine reliably prevents or reverses typical seborrheic keratoses.
   - No change to COPD or osteoarthritis medications is justified from the supplied information. Obtain a complete prescription, over-the-counter, and supplement list before prescribing anything; interactions cannot be assessed without it.
   - Do not use home freezing devices, acids, or wart-removal preparations on these lesions before confirmation, particularly on an atypical pigmented lesion.

4. **Procedures**
   - **Diagnostic skin biopsy** only as indicated above.
   - Once confirmed benign, no removal is medically necessary unless lesions are irritated, bleeding from friction, or otherwise troublesome. A dermatologist can offer **cryotherapy, shave removal, or curettage**, discussing scarring and pigment changes.
   - Avoid destructive treatment of a suspicious lesion before obtaining a tissue diagnosis.

5. **Referrals**
   - **Dermatology within approximately 2–4 weeks** to confirm the eruptive pattern and identify any lesions requiring biopsy.
   - **Expedite dermatology to within 1–2 weeks** if an individual lesion is suspicious for melanoma or another skin cancer.
   - Gastroenterology or another organ-specific specialty is indicated if symptoms, examination, or testing suggests an internal malignancy. **Oncology referral is not indicated solely for multiple seborrheic keratoses** without evidence of cancer.

6. **Counseling and warning signs**
   - Explain that these are usually benign “stuck-on” growths and are not contagious. The concern is the **speed and extent of appearance**, not that ordinary seborrheic keratoses themselves turn cancerous.
   - The Leser–Trélat association is uncommon and debated because both seborrheic keratoses and cancer become more common with age. Evaluation should be thoughtful rather than assuming cancer or pursuing indiscriminate scans.
   - Ask her to photograph the affected area now, ideally with help and consistent lighting, to document progression.
   - Seek prompt review for continued rapid spread, persistent unexplained itching, weight loss, early satiety, swallowing difficulty, new bowel changes, postmenopausal bleeding, or a lesion that changes substantially or bleeds spontaneously.
   - **Urgent same-day assessment** is warranted for hemoptysis, black stools, or significant unexplained bleeding. **Emergency care** is appropriate for substantial bleeding, fainting, severe breathlessness, or chest pain.
   - If still smoking, advise cessation and offer support; do not presume current smoking from the history.

7. **Follow-up and monitoring**
   - **Primary care should coordinate the work-up** and review examination findings, screening status, and any ordered laboratory results within **2–4 weeks**, sooner for abnormalities.
   - Obtain and act on any biopsy result promptly, generally within **1–2 weeks of biopsy**.
   - If dermatology confirms benign lesions and the initial assessment is reassuring, reassess symptoms and lesion progression in about **3 months**. There is no validated program of serial scans or tumor-marker surveillance for this finding.

8. **Contingencies**
   - **If lesions are typical and longstanding rather than truly eruptive:** reassure and continue routine cancer screening.
   - **If CBC shows anemia:** characterize it with indices and, when appropriate, ferritin and iron studies. Confirmed unexplained iron-deficiency anemia at this age generally warrants gastrointestinal evaluation, commonly colonoscopy and upper endoscopy, especially if postmenopausal.
   - **If dysphagia, gastrointestinal bleeding, persistent early satiety, or unexplained weight loss develops:** expedite diagnostic evaluation and gastroenterology referral. Unintentional loss of **more than 5% of body weight over 6–12 months** is a clear concern, though smaller losses with other symptoms also warrant assessment.
   - **If lesions continue to erupt rapidly despite a reassuring initial evaluation:** repeat the history and examination with dermatology and primary care, and consider targeted imaging or endoscopy based on the evolving findings—not automatic whole-body screening.

## Recommendation set 1

**Assessment:** Seborrheic keratoses (SKs) are common and benign at 57, but a clear surge in number over a few months is not the usual pattern. It raises the possibility of the Leser-Trélat sign, a rare paraneoplastic phenomenon most often linked to GI adenocarcinoma (especially gastric and colorectal), and also to lung, breast, and lymphoproliferative cancers. Most patients with a surge turn out to have no malignancy, so the plan is a targeted, tiered evaluation rather than a broad scan, plus close follow-up.

**1. Visit now (within 1–2 weeks): history, exam, baseline documentation**
- Define the eruption: onset date, rate of new lesions, itching (often present in Leser-Trélat), and whether lesions are inflamed or changing.
- Ask about constitutional symptoms: unintentional weight loss (compare with prior recorded weights), appetite loss, early satiety, fever, night sweats, fatigue.
- Ask about GI symptoms: dyspepsia, dysphagia, abdominal pain, change in bowel habit, rectal bleeding, black stools.
- Ask about chest symptoms: hemoptysis, new cough, or change in her COPD pattern.
- Ask about breast symptoms and family history of GI, breast, and other cancers.
- Review medications and supplements for new drugs in the past year. Biologics (e.g., adalimumab) and G-CSF are rare triggers of eruptive SKs. Her levothyroxine and COPD inhalers are not recognized causes.
- Verify smoking status and true pack-years. 10 pack-years with COPD is a small exposure, so ask about occupational and environmental exposures.
- Examine:
  - Full skin exam, including mucosa, nails, and scalp.
  - Dermoscopy of lesions, since melanoma can mimic SK.
  - Acanthosis nigricans (neck, axillae, groin) and "tripe palms" (velvety palms). These strongly raise suspicion for a paraneoplastic process.
  - Lymph nodes (cervical, supraclavicular, axillary, inguinal), breast exam, abdomen (mass, liver edge, spleen), thyroid.
- Record weight and take standardized baseline photographs of the back. Count or map the lesions so progression can be measured objectively.
- Biopsy (shave or punch) any lesion that is atypical, pigmented with irregular features, inflamed, bleeding, or rapidly changing. Do not assume all lesions are SKs.

**2. Initial tests (order at the first visit)**
- CBC with differential: look for anemia, eosinophilia, and lymphocyte abnormalities.
- Ferritin and iron studies. Note that chronic hypoxemia from COPD can mask anemia by raising hemoglobin.
- CMP: liver enzymes, alkaline phosphatase, calcium, creatinine.
- LDH, ESR/CRP, HbA1c or fasting glucose (acanthosis nigricans and insulin resistance), TSH (annual check, reassuring if stable).
- One-time hepatitis C and HIV screening if not yet done. HIV is a recognized cause of eruptive SKs.
- Alpha-1 antitrypsin level (one-time, recommended for all COPD patients, especially with low smoking exposure).
- Chest X-ray (PA/lateral) if none in the past 12 months. This is a low-cost check given COPD and the paraneoplastic concern.
- Spirometry, if post-bronchodilator confirmation of COPD is not on file.

**3. Cancer screening: confirm each is current, and complete any that are overdue**
- Colorectal: if no colonoscopy has been done (or it was more than 10 years ago, or surveillance is due), arrange colonoscopy within about 4–6 weeks. It is indicated for age anyway and also serves as part of the paraneoplastic work-up. Use FIT only if colonoscopy is declined.
- Breast: screening mammogram if not done within the past 2 years.
- Cervical: Pap/HPV per guideline interval.
- Lung: she does not meet USPSTF criteria for low-dose CT screening at 10 pack-years (criteria: age 50–80, ≥20 pack-years, current smoker or quit within 15 years). If the corrected history reaches ≥20 pack-years, enroll her in annual LDCT.

**4. Conditional escalation of the work-up (explicit thresholds)**
- Upper endoscopy (EGD) within 2–4 weeks if any of the following:
  - Dyspepsia, dysphagia, early satiety, or epigastric pain.
  - Iron-deficiency anemia (ferritin <30 ng/mL, or Hb <12 g/dL).
  - Unintentional weight loss.
  - Acanthosis nigricans or tripe palms.
- CT chest/abdomen/pelvis with contrast within 2 weeks if any of the following:
  - Unintentional weight loss ≥5% of body weight in 6 months.
  - Persistent lymphadenopathy (>1 cm for >4 weeks, or any supraclavicular node).
  - Hepatomegaly or an abdominal mass.
  - Unexplained elevated alkaline phosphatase, calcium, or LDH.
  - Hemoptysis or an abnormal chest X-ray.
- Hematology/oncology referral (urgent, within 1–2 weeks) if imaging, labs, or endoscopy are abnormal, or if the CBC suggests a lymphoproliferative process.
- If all of the above are negative but lesions keep rapidly increasing, or itching or new skin signs (acanthosis, tripe palms) develop: repeat the history, exam, labs, and chest X-ray, and obtain CT chest/abdomen/pelvis rather than reassuring her.

**5. Referral: Dermatology**
- Routine-expedited (within 2–4 weeks) for confirmation of diagnosis, dermoscopy, biopsy of any suspicious lesion, and review of the eruption pattern.
- Upgrade to urgent (within 1 week) if there are atypical or pigmented lesions that cannot be excluded as melanoma, or if there is acanthosis nigricans, tripe palms, or diffuse pruritic eruption.

**6. Treatment of the lesions**
- SKs are benign and need no treatment. Do not remove them as a substitute for the evaluation.
- Removal (cryotherapy, curettage) is only for symptomatic, irritated, or cosmetically bothersome lesions, done by dermatology or in clinic after the work-up is under way.
- For itching: fragrance-free emollient twice daily. Add a low-potency topical steroid (e.g., hydrocortisone 1% twice daily for up to 2 weeks) for inflamed lesions. Persistent or severe itching needs reassessment, not just treatment, because it is a red flag in this context.
- Sun protection (SPF 30+, protective clothing) and monthly self skin checks.

**7. COPD and thyroid: continue usual care**
- Continue levothyroxine at the current dose, with TSH every 12 months (sooner if symptoms or weight change).
- COPD: confirm inhaler technique and adherence, and review the action plan.
- Vaccinations: annual influenza, COVID-19 per current schedule, pneumococcal (PCV20 or PCV21 once), RSV (age 50–59 with chronic lung disease is eligible per current recommendations), Tdap if due, and recombinant zoster (Shingrix).
- If she smokes, offer cessation counseling and pharmacotherapy: varenicline 0.5 mg daily for 3 days, then 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days, then 1 mg twice daily for 12 weeks, with an option to extend. Nicotine replacement is an alternative. Set a quit date.

**8. Follow-up schedule (primary care)**
- 1–2 weeks: review results and decide on escalation per item 4.
- 4–6 weeks: confirm colonoscopy/mammogram/other screening are completed and dermatology has seen her.
- 3 months: repeat skin count and photographs, weight, symptom review, CBC and ferritin.
- 6 months: repeat the same assessment and review again for red flags.
- 12 months: full reassessment, plus annual TSH and COPD review.
- If the eruption stabilizes or stops, no further cancer work-up beyond routine screening is needed. If new lesions keep appearing at the 3- or 6-month visit, re-escalate per item 4.

**9. What I tell the patient**
- Most SKs are harmless, but a sudden increase in number can occasionally signal an underlying internal condition, including cancer. The likelihood is low, but we will check carefully.
- Even if the tests are normal, I will keep checking at 3, 6, and 12 months. A normal initial work-up does not end the follow-up.
- If a cancer were found and treated, the SKs may fade.
- Do not scratch or pick at lesions.

**10. Return precautions (come in within days, or go to urgent care for severe symptoms)**
- Unintentional weight loss of more than 5 lb in a month, or ≥5% in 6 months.
- Persistent abdominal pain, difficulty or pain swallowing, vomiting, or early fullness.
- Blood in stool, black stools, or a change in bowel habits lasting more than 2–3 weeks.
- Coughing up blood, new persistent cough, or worsening breathlessness beyond her COPD baseline.
- Night sweats, fevers, or new lumps in the neck, armpit, groin, or breast.
- Skin darkening or thickening in the armpits or neck, thickened palms, or intense itching.
- Any mole or spot that changes in color, shape, or size, bleeds, or does not heal.
- Rapid new lesion growth, or a sudden jump in numbers.

## Recommendation set 2

This is a rapid eruption of presumed seborrheic keratoses, which is not simply dismissed as routine aging until the diagnosis is confirmed. Multiple abruptly appearing seborrheic keratoses can represent the (uncommon and debated) sign of Leser–Trélat, sometimes associated with internal malignancy, but most cases are benign or “pseudo–Leser–Trélat.”

1. **Arrange dermatology assessment promptly (ideally within 2–4 weeks; sooner if any lesion is changing rapidly, bleeding, painful, ulcerated, or distinctly different from the others).**  
   - Request a **full-body skin examination with dermoscopy** to confirm that these are seborrheic keratoses and not melanoma, pigmented basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, or another eruption.  
   - **Biopsy (shave or punch as appropriate) at least one representative lesion** if the clinical diagnosis is uncertain or any lesion has atypical pigment pattern, asymmetry, irregular border/color, ulceration, or rapid individual change.  
   - Clinical photographs/count documentation are useful for monitoring progression.

2. **Perform a focused review for malignancy-associated symptoms and signs now.** Ask specifically about:
   - Unintentional weight loss, fevers, drenching night sweats, fatigue, anorexia.
   - New dysphagia, early satiety, persistent reflux, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, change in bowel habit, melena/hematochezia, iron-deficiency symptoms.
   - Persistent cough, hemoptysis, worsening dyspnea beyond COPD baseline, chest pain.
   - Breast mass/nipple changes, postmenopausal bleeding, pelvic symptoms, urinary blood.
   - New generalized pruritus, acanthosis nigricans, enlarged lymph nodes, hepatosplenomegaly, or other paraneoplastic skin findings.
   - Also review recent medications and inflammatory skin eruptions, because “pseudo–Leser–Trélat” eruptions can occur without cancer.

3. **Complete a careful physical examination, including lymph nodes, breast examination when appropriate, abdominal examination, and inspection for acanthosis nigricans or other suspicious skin findings.** Any palpable mass, lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, focal pulmonary finding, or concerning symptom should trigger an expedited, organ-directed evaluation rather than nonspecific testing.

4. **Ensure she is up to date on evidence-based cancer screening; do not order broad tumor-marker panels or whole-body imaging solely because of seborrheic keratoses.**
   - **Colorectal cancer screening:** If not current, arrange either **FIT annually** or **screening colonoscopy every 10 years** (or another guideline-concordant option). Given this presentation, colonoscopy is reasonable if she is overdue, has gastrointestinal symptoms, positive FIT, anemia, or a relevant family history.
   - **Breast cancer screening:** Confirm a screening mammogram has been completed within the recommended interval (commonly every 1–2 years depending on the applicable guideline and prior results); order if overdue.
   - **Cervical cancer screening:** If she has a cervix and has not met exit criteria, confirm current screening—e.g., **primary high-risk HPV testing every 5 years**, HPV/Pap cotesting every 5 years, or cytology every 3 years through age 65, as applicable.
   - **Lung cancer screening:** She does **not** meet standard annual low-dose CT eligibility based on the provided 10-pack-year history (usual threshold is ≥20 pack-years in eligible age groups). Do not obtain screening LDCT unless additional smoking exposure history changes eligibility. Obtain diagnostic chest imaging only for pulmonary red flags or a meaningful change from COPD baseline.

5. **Order diagnostic tests only if supported by history/examination.**
   - If systemic symptoms, gastrointestinal symptoms, pallor, or concern for occult blood loss are present: obtain **CBC with differential, ferritin/iron studies, comprehensive metabolic panel**, and prompt GI-directed testing/referral.  
   - If persistent cough, hemoptysis, unexplained weight loss, focal chest findings, or significant unexplained COPD worsening is present: obtain a **diagnostic chest radiograph initially**, followed by **contrast chest CT** if abnormal or if clinical concern remains high.

   - **6 and 12 months:** repeat history, weight, and exam, and update photographs, even if the initial work-up is negative. A paraneoplastic sign can precede the cancer by months. Repeat CBC and CMP at 6 months.
   - Keep routine COPD follow-up (spirometry, inhaler technique, vaccines for influenza, COVID-19, pneumococcal, RSV, and Tdap per schedule) separate from this workup.

10. **Contingency thresholds.**
    - **Work-up positive** (colonoscopy mass, abnormal imaging, or biopsy showing malignancy): urgent referral within 1 week to the appropriate oncologic service (GI/surgical oncology, breast, pulmonology/thoracic oncology, or hematology), with staging per specialty. Tell her SKs may regress with cancer treatment, and recurrence can signal relapse.
    - **Iron-deficiency anemia** (Hb below 12 g/dL with low ferritin): colonoscopy and EGD within 2 weeks.
    - **Weight loss of 5% or more in 6 months**, or other alarm features: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis within 2 weeks and upper plus lower endoscopy.
    - **Abnormal LFTs, calcium, LDH, or CRP:** targeted imaging, and consider hematology/oncology input if LDH is elevated with lymphadenopathy.
    - **Lymphadenopathy** persisting beyond 2–4 weeks or any node over 1.5 cm: imaging and excisional or core biopsy.
    - **Biopsy showing melanoma or another skin cancer:** same-week referral to dermatology/surgical oncology per pathology.
    - **HIV positive:** begin HIV care pathway.
    - **Work-up negative at 12 months and SKs stable:** return to routine screening. If new rapid eruption recurs at any time, repeat the evaluation.
    - **Persistent generalized pruritus or erythroderma:** dermatology review sooner.

11. **What to tell the patient and what to watch for.** Call within 48 hours, or come in, for:
    - Black or bloody stools, blood in stool, or persistent change in bowel habit
    - Unintentional weight loss, new difficulty swallowing, persistent vomiting, or early fullness
    - Coughing blood, a new persistent cough, or worsening dyspnea beyond her COPD baseline
    - Night sweats, fevers, or new lumps in the neck, armpit, groin, or breast
    - Any lesion that bleeds, ulcerates, darkens, has irregular borders or multiple colors, or changes quickly
    - Dark, velvety thickening in skin folds or thickened palms, or severe generalized itching

    Ask her to keep scheduled appointments, especially the colonoscopy, and to take photographs of her back monthly, using a helper or mirror, to track change.

12. **Communication and documentation.** Record that Leser-Trélat is on the differential. Give her a written list of pending tests and referrals, and a direct contact for results. Confirm she understands why the colonoscopy and dermatology visit are expedited. Use a closed-loop tracking system for all orders.

This is not the usual gradual appearance of seborrheic keratoses with aging. A rapid eruption of multiple lesions over 4 months raises concern for an eruptive seborrheic keratosis pattern (possible sign of Leser-Trélat), which is often benign but can rarely be associated with occult malignancy; the lesions should first be confirmed clinically and any atypical lesion excluded as melanoma or another skin cancer.

1. **Arrange expedited dermatology referral (ideally within 2–4 weeks).**

2. **Perform a focused history and examination now for occult cancer or systemic illness.** Specifically ask/document:  
   - Unintentional weight loss, anorexia, fatigue, fevers, night sweats.  
   - Dysphagia, persistent reflux, early satiety, abdominal pain, change in bowel habits, melena/hematochezia, iron-deficiency symptoms.  
   - New breast mass/discharge, postmenopausal bleeding, pelvic/abdominal bloating.  
   - Persistent cough different from COPD baseline, hemoptysis, chest pain, hoarseness, or new/worsening dyspnea.

3. **Ensure she is fully up to date with routine, evidence-based cancer screening; do not order tumor markers or indiscriminate whole-body imaging.**  
   - **Colorectal cancer:** If she is not current with screening, arrange **colonoscopy** (preferred if there are GI symptoms, anemia, positive stool test, or strong concern), or annual **FIT** if average risk and asymptomatic. A positive FIT requires diagnostic colonoscopy.  
   - **Breast cancer:** Confirm mammography is current; if not, order a screening mammogram now.  
   - **Cervical cancer:** If she has a cervix and has not met criteria to stop screening, confirm current HPV-based testing/cytology per local guidelines.  
   - **Lung cancer screening:** She does **not** meet standard annual low-dose CT screening criteria based on the stated 10-pack-year history (usual threshold is at least 20 pack-years). Do not order low-dose CT solely for smoking history. Order a **diagnostic chest CT** only if concerning respiratory symptoms, abnormal examination, or abnormal chest radiograph warrant it.

4. **Order targeted baseline tests if not recently available or if history/exam raises concern.**  
   - CBC with differential, including hemoglobin and indices.  
   - Comprehensive metabolic panel, including liver enzymes and calcium.  
   - Ferritin/iron studies if anemia, fatigue, GI symptoms, or microcytosis is present.

   - Explain that seborrheic keratoses are common and usually harmless, but the abrupt increase justifies prompt confirmation and review of routine cancer screening. This finding alone does not diagnose cancer.

7. **Return/urgent-evaluation precautions.**  
   - Seek prompt assessment for bleeding or ulcerating skin lesions, rapidly changing pigmented lesions, new generalized severe itch, unexplained weight loss, persistent vomiting, black/bloody stools, dysphagia, hemoptysis, a new breast mass, postmenopausal bleeding, or worsening respiratory symptoms beyond her usual COPD baseline.

## Recommendation set 3

Seborrheic keratoses are common, benign growths at age 57, but a marked increase over only four months should not simply be dismissed as normal aging. This can be a benign eruption, but it warrants assessment for the **sign of Leser–Trélat**—a rare, sometimes cancer-associated eruption of seborrheic keratoses; the skin finding alone neither diagnoses cancer nor establishes that association.

1. **Diagnosis and its severity**
   - Working diagnosis: **rapidly increasing presumed seborrheic keratoses**, requiring confirmation by examination.
   - Determine whether these are genuinely new lesions or previously unnoticed lesions. Review photographs if available and ask about itching, inflammation, bleeding, and growth elsewhere.
   - Leser–Trélat is an association of abrupt, numerous seborrheic keratoses with internal malignancy, classically gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma. Its specificity is uncertain because both seborrheic keratoses and cancer become more common with age.
   - This is **not an emergency based on the information given**, but the rapid change warrants prompt outpatient evaluation.

2. **Tests: confirmation, dangerous alternatives, and pretreatment baselines**
   - Arrange an in-person assessment, including a **complete skin examination with dermoscopy of atypical lesions**, rather than assuming every lesion on the back is a seborrheic keratosis.
   - Document lesion distribution and representative photographs. Examine for lymphadenopathy, abdominal masses, and associated skin findings such as newly extensive acanthosis nigricans.
   - Ask specifically about unintended weight loss, reduced appetite, early satiety, dysphagia, persistent abdominal pain, altered bowel habits, black or bloody stools, fever/night sweats, and new or changed respiratory symptoms. Review personal/family cancer history, prior screening, current medications, and any treatment started before the eruption.
   - **Biopsy any diagnostically uncertain or atypical lesion**, particularly one with asymmetric pigmentation, ulceration, spontaneous bleeding, or growth unlike the others, to exclude melanoma or another skin cancer. Biopsy can establish seborrheic keratosis but cannot establish its relationship to internal cancer.
   - If the eruption is confirmed as abrupt, extensive, and unexplained, obtain **CBC with differential and comprehensive metabolic panel** as an initial assessment. Add iron studies if anemia is present. Normal results do not exclude malignancy.
   - Verify and update routine screening:
     - **Colorectal:** at 57, screening should be current. If average-risk and overdue, offer colonoscopy or annual fecal immunochemical testing according to local guidance and preference. Symptoms or iron-deficiency anemia require diagnostic evaluation rather than a screening stool test.
     - **Breast:** ensure screening mammography is current.
     - **Cervical:** ensure screening is current if she has a cervix and remains eligible.
     - A **10-pack-year history does not meet the usual ≥20-pack-year threshold for screening low-dose chest CT**, even with COPD. New concerning respiratory symptoms require diagnostic evaluation separately.
   - Do not routinely order tumor-marker panels, PET scans, whole-body CT, or upper endoscopy solely because of these lesions. Additional testing should follow symptoms, examination, screening gaps, or a particularly convincing unexplained eruption after dermatology review.
   - No medication-specific pretreatment laboratory testing is currently needed.

3. **Medications: start, stop, hold, or adjust**
   - **No systemic or topical medication is indicated solely to treat asymptomatic seborrheic keratoses or to prevent a possible associated cancer.**
   - Continue prescribed COPD treatment; there is no basis here to stop inhalers or other necessary medication.
   - Obtain the actual medication list before attributing the eruption to a drug or prescribing symptom treatment. No patient-specific interaction assessment is possible from the information provided.

4. **Procedures**
   - **Skin biopsy** as above for suspicious or uncertain lesions; do not destroy a suspicious pigmented lesion before obtaining a diagnosis.
   - Once confirmed benign, bothersome lesions may be treated with cryotherapy, shave removal, or curettage. Removal is optional and does not address any possible internal association.
   - No immediate invasive internal investigation is mandatory from the skin finding alone.

5. **Referrals: specialty and urgency**
   - **Dermatology within approximately 2–4 weeks** for diagnostic confirmation and assessment of the eruption.
   - Use an **urgent suspected-skin-cancer pathway, ideally within 1–2 weeks**, if any individual lesion is suspicious.
   - Gastroenterology or another organ-specific referral should be expedited if symptoms, iron-deficiency anemia, examination findings, or other tests suggest malignancy.
   - Oncology referral is not indicated without evidence of cancer.

6. **Counseling and warning signs**
   - Explain that ordinary seborrheic keratoses are benign and **do not themselves turn into internal cancer**. Rapid multiplication deserves evaluation, but most such lesions do not establish a cancer diagnosis.
   - Avoid picking lesions or using home freezing/acid products before confirmation.
   - Report unexplained weight loss, persistent abdominal symptoms, swallowing difficulty, new lymph-node enlargement, or bleeding/changing skin lesions promptly.
   - Seek urgent care for vomiting blood, black stools with weakness or faintness, significant coughing of blood, or severe/new breathlessness beyond her COPD baseline.
   - Confirm smoking status and offer cessation support if she still smokes.

7. **Follow-up and monitoring**
   - Primary care should review the history, examination, screening status, and any laboratory results **within 2–4 weeks**, coordinating with dermatology.
   - Reassess lesion progression and systemic symptoms **in approximately 8–12 weeks** if the initial evaluation is reassuring.
   - There is no validated schedule for repeated cancer scans in an otherwise well patient with a negative evaluation; continue routine screening and symptom-directed reassessment.

8. **Contingencies**
   - **If iron-deficiency anemia, gastrointestinal bleeding, progressive dysphagia, or unintentional weight loss exceeding roughly 5% over six months is found:** arrange expedited diagnostic investigation; gastrointestinal evaluation may require colonoscopy and/or upper endoscopy.
   - **If new hemoptysis or persistent unexplained respiratory change occurs:** investigate diagnostically rather than attributing it automatically to COPD.
   - **If the eruption continues rapidly despite an unrevealing initial assessment:** dermatology and primary care should reconsider alternative diagnoses and whether individualized internal-malignancy investigation is warranted.
   - **If lesions are confirmed as ordinary seborrheic keratoses, screening is current, and no concerning features emerge:** reassure and observe rather than subjecting her to indiscriminate cancer testing.

## Recommendation set 1

**Assessment:** This is most consistent with capecitabine-induced hand-foot syndrome (palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia), likely grade 2 and borderline grade 3 if it limits self-care. CKD may be raising his capecitabine exposure. Oral prednisone is not first-line, so I would not start it now. Treatment is to hold capecitabine, give local skin care and analgesia, and exclude mimics.

**1. Prednisone: do not start now**
- Systemic steroids are not standard for capecitabine hand-foot syndrome. The evidence is weak, and the main treatment is interrupting or reducing the drug.
- In an 82-year-old with metastatic cancer on chemotherapy, steroids add risks: infection through fissured skin, hyperglycemia, fluid retention and BP rise, GI bleeding, delirium, and masking of fever.
- Revisit only with oncology if he has grade 3 disease (blistering, ulceration, can't walk or use his hands) that persists after a drug hold and optimized topical care. Even then it would be a short, defined course.

**2. Same-day call to his oncologist**
- Report that he has grade 2-3 hand-foot syndrome and ask for approval to hold capecitabine now. Until I hear back, advise him to hold it and not to take more doses.
- Hold until symptoms are grade 0-1, usually 1-2 weeks. Resumption and dose are oncology's decision. Per the label, the first occurrence at grade 2 resumes at full dose, a second occurrence at 75%, a third at 50%, and a fourth means stopping. A grade 3 first occurrence resumes at 75%.
- Ask whether oxaliplatin on the next cycle date should proceed. The oxaliplatin schedule is oncology's decision.
- Ask them to confirm the capecitabine dose against his renal function. Capecitabine is contraindicated at CrCl <30 mL/min, and the dose should be 75% at CrCl 30-50.
- Ask about the unusual regimen for prostate cancer, in case the primary diagnosis or histology is different.

**3. Tests today**
- CBC with differential.
- CMP (creatinine/eGFR, K, Ca, LFTs, bilirubin, glucose) and magnesium. Calculate Cockcroft-Gault CrCl.
- Uric acid, CRP and ESR.
- INR only if he takes warfarin, because of the capecitabine interaction. Review the full medication list.
- ECG if he has any chest pain or palpitations, since capecitabine can cause coronary vasospasm and he has CAD.
- Culture any purulent or weeping fissure. Check the web spaces and nails for tinea.
- Hand and foot X-rays only if bony tenderness or digital clubbing is present, or if symptoms persist after the drug hold. This looks for hypertrophic osteoarthropathy from the lung metastases.
- Aspirate any single hot, swollen joint for crystals and culture, because gout or pseudogout is possible with CKD.
- Ask about DPD deficiency features: severe diarrhea, mucositis, or low counts together with the skin toxicity. If present, this is urgent and capecitabine stays off pending oncology.

**4. Skin care and pain control**
- Urea 20-40% cream BID-TID to the palms and soles. Use 10% or plain petrolatum on open fissures, since higher strengths sting.
- Clobetasol 0.05% ointment BID to the red or thickened intact skin for up to 2 weeks, not on open fissures. Review for skin atrophy.
- Seal deep fissures with liquid bandage or hydrocolloid dressing.
- Overnight, apply thick emollient and wear cotton gloves and socks.
- Acetaminophen 650 mg q6h, maximum 3 g/day. Add lidocaine 4% topical for focal pain.
- If pain is neuropathic and severe, gabapentin 100 mg at bedtime, titrated cautiously for CKD. Avoid oral NSAIDs because of CKD, CAD, and HTN. Avoid topical diclofenac over large areas.
- Pyridoxine is optional. Evidence is mixed, so I would not rely on it.

**5. Pantoprazole**
- It is not the cause, since symptoms started first.
- PPIs may reduce capecitabine absorption, though the data are mixed. Check the indication and tell oncology.
- If there is no strong indication, stop it. If acid suppression is needed, famotidine with a renal dose is an alternative.

**6. Follow-up (what, when, who)**
- **48-72 hours:** nurse phone call, and a clinic visit if pain is uncontrolled.
- **1 week:** my visit to re-grade the skin, check function and gait, review the repeat CBC and BMP, and confirm what oncology decided.
- **Weekly during the hold:** repeat visit or phone call until grade ≤1.
- **Before each 3-week cycle:** labs with oncology, including creatinine for dose adjustment.
- **Every visit:** recheck CrCl, fall risk, and the skin.

**7. Referrals**
- **Oncology:** same day, as above.
- **Podiatry:** within 2 weeks for fissures and hyperkeratosis, with supportive footwear and cushioned insoles.
- **Dermatology:** within 1-2 weeks if grade 3 or not improving by 7 days after the hold.
- **PT/OT:** within 2 weeks if grip, gait, or self-care is limited. Do a home safety and falls assessment.
- **Palliative care:** routine referral within 2-4 weeks for symptom support. Hold a goals-of-care conversation in line with his overall prognosis and oncology plan.

**8. Contingencies with thresholds**
- **No improvement 7 days after the hold, or worsening:** call oncology and dermatology, and consider a short steroid course with oncology only if grade 3.
- **Blistering, moist desquamation, ulceration, or inability to walk, grip, or dress:** same-day evaluation.
- **Fever ≥38.0°C (100.4°F):** ED the same day for possible neutropenic fever.
- **Spreading redness, warmth, pus, or red streaks:** treat as cellulitis. Culture first, then start renally dosed cephalexin or other appropriate coverage. If he is systemically ill, send him to the ED.
- **Diarrhea ≥4 stools/day above baseline, mouth sores, or poor oral intake:** stop capecitabine and call the same day. Dehydration can cause AKI in CKD, so repeat the BMP.
- **CrCl <30:** capecitabine is contraindicated, so notify oncology. **CrCl 30-50:** he needs the 75% dose.
- **Chest pain or pressure:** call 911. Capecitabine vasospasm is possible.
- **Hot single joint, or uric acid high with a gout-like pattern:** aspirate, and treat with a renally dosed regimen if crystals are found.

**9. What to tell the patient and family**
- This is a known, usually reversible side effect of capecitabine. It is not an allergy, it is not contagious, and it does not mean the cancer is worse.
- Take no capecitabine until oncology says to restart. Never take extra doses. If he restarts, he should take it within 30 minutes after meals, 12 hours apart.
- Use lukewarm water and pat the skin dry. Moisturize several times a day and after every handwashing.
- Avoid heat, friction, tight shoes, prolonged standing or walking, heavy gripping, and adhesives.
- Wear cushioned cotton socks and loose shoes. Inspect his feet daily, or have a family member do it.
- Avoid cold exposure, because oxaliplatin causes cold sensitivity.
- Do not use OTC NSAIDs or start steroids on his own.
- Call or come in for fever, spreading redness or pus, blisters or open sores, severe diarrhea, mouth sores, reduced urine, or chest pain.
- Bring all medications and the chemotherapy calendar to each visit.

   - **Treating oncology team: today**, to coordinate the chemotherapy hold, renal-dose review, and restart plan.
